title: Do This If You Want Another Year of Windows 10 Security Updates
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Michal Krakowiak/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft is offering another year of Windows 10 security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027.
                                            If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action.
                                            Other users can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you are still holding on to Windows 10, there's good news: Microsoft is offering another year of security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027. Microsoft officially ended support for the older OS last year but allowed users to join the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in order to maintain protection against viruses and hackers. ESU coverage was supposed to expire on Oct. 13, 2026, but the company is allowing enrolled Windows 10 users to receive monthly patches for another year—and it's not too late to sign up if you haven't already.  You can stay on Windows 10 through Oct. 2027If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action on your part. If you haven't, though, you can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year. To be eligible, your device must be running Windows 10 version 22H2 Home, Professional, Pro Education, or Workstations editions and have the latest Windows update installed. You must also be signed into a Microsoft account with administrator status. 
Windows users were originally able to purchase ESU coverage for $30, and Microsoft later added the option to either redeem 1,000 Microsoft Rewards points or opt into Windows Backup to get protection for free. To check your coverage or sign up, go to Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update and look for an ESU enrollment link (visible if your device is eligible). Follow the prompts to sign into your Microsoft account and choose your enrollment option. If you've already purchased an ESU license, you can apply it to up to 10 devices running Windows 10 as long as they are linked to your Microsoft account. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The ESU program does not include any new features or non-security updates, but if you want to stay on Windows 10, it's highly recommended that you enroll in the program. Microsoft has started pushing hundreds of critical security fixes each month—a handful of which have been actively exploited zero-days—so you should ensure your device stays protected for as long as possible.

title: Apple Has a Fix for Your New Apple Watch's Restart Bug
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Annice Lyn/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just fixed an issue with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 that caused random reboots.
                                            Many users noted their watches were unexpectedly restarting. According to MacRumors, the watch's Neural Engine appears to be timing out.
                                            Apple didn't explain what it changed to fix the issue, but watchOS 27.0.1 does include a patch. This update is exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and the Ultra 4, should be the "best" smartwatches the company has to offer. While they're minor upgrades over the Series 11 and Ultra 3, there are some key improvements, including the new S11 chip and a heart rate monitor that checks your pulse every five seconds. If you picked up one of these watches, you might have put these new upgrades to the test—that is, if your watch didn't restart on you. As reported by MacRumors, Apple's latest smartwatches appear prone to unexpected restarts. That's according to numerous posts on the site's forums, with users saying their watches abruptly show a blank screen with the Apple logo. There doesn't appear to be any particular action that triggers it: Users say their watches rebooted when recording a workout, using Siri AI, editing watch faces, or using the Maps app. Many users on this Reddit thread share similar experiences with their new watches. Some users dug deeper, pulling their Apple Watches' diagnostics at the time of rebooting. Rather than a specific function, the culprit appears to be a timeout with the Neural Engine, the hardware that processes Apple's AI features.  Users tried multiple workarounds themselves: One Redditor simply turned the watch off and on themself, and the issue never returned; others tried resetting the watch as new, but experienced rebooting again. MacRumors highlighted one case where a user received a replacement from Apple, and it, too, rebooted unexpectedly. It does appear to be an issue with the Series 12 and Ultra 4, and, luckily, Apple figured it out. 
watchOS 27.0.1 fixes unexpected reboots with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4On Wednesday, Apple unexpectedly released watchOS 27.0.1. The update has a brief changelog, with only one new addition: "This update provides bug fixes for your Apple Watch, including fixing an issue where Apple Watch may restart unexpectedly." Apple didn't clarify exactly what it changed to fix the issue, but at least the reboots should be over. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
This update is only for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 users, so don't expect to see it unless you have one of Apple's newest wearables. If you do, make sure to install it as soon as possible to avoid dealing with these unexpected restarts. To install watchOS 27.0.1, head to the Apple Watch app, then tap My Watch and go to General > Software Update.

        If you want an advanced fitness tracker in a sleek package, Garmin makes some of the best options for detailed health and workout insights, along with longer battery life than many mainstream smartwatches. One of its most enticing models is the Garmin Vivoactive 6, which is currently down to a record-low $229.99 (originally $299.99) on Amazon.
Its 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen is crisp and easier to read than Garmin’s older display technology. It’s also lightweight at 36 grams with the included band and slim, at just 10.9 mm thick. As a result, it’s a better option for overnight wear and sleep tracking than the bulkier Venu. The watch also has a Smart Wake Alarm, which uses a half-hour window to try to wake you during a lighter sleep stage with vibration, giving users a more pleasant way to wake up than a blaring phone alarm.  The watch lasts up to 11 days in smartwatch mode, removing the need to charge it nightly, and it delivers up to 21 hours of battery life in GPS-only mode. Built-in GPS lets you accurately track outdoor workouts and activities without bringing your phone, while music storage allows for phone-free listening with compatible Bluetooth headphones. It also features Garmin Pay for contactless payments, so you can leave your wallet behind, too.With more than 80 preloaded sports apps, the Vivoactive 6 is highly versatile and supports a wide range of workouts. It’s also a solid option for strength training, with tools to track reps, sets, and rest periods, plus step-by-step workouts for strength, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, mobility, and more. Beyond health and fitness tracking, it includes Garmin Coach plans that adapt to your performance and health metrics, plus daily suggested workouts.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It doesn’t have every feature serious runners and adventurers may want from the brand’s pricier watches, such as more advanced training and navigation tools. But it packs a ton of useful features into a lightweight, everyday-friendly design and lets you spend more time away from your phone if that’s the goal. At $70 off, the Garmin Vivoactive 6 is a great choice for iPhone and Android users who want a capable fitness smartwatch without the premium Garmin price tag.

title: I Tried Snap Specs, and They Could Be the Future of Smart Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 25, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Stephen Johnson
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Meta to the market by five years. Meta’s Ray-Bans and Oakleys captured massive consumer mindshare anyway, while Snap’s smart eyewear has been less visible. With Snap Specs, though, the company is aiming to make up for lost time by delivering smart glasses that go beyond a hidden camera and voice-activated AI. At the Snapdragon 2026 Summit, I got my hands (and eyes) on a pair of Snap’s soon-to-be-released spatial-computing glasses that overlay digital graphics onto the physical world.Specs are heavy on tech but light on your face
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
There's a lot of tech packed into these black polymer frames. They're powered by two Snapdragon processors, with two full-color hi-res cameras facing outward; the tracking system supports 6DOF (six degrees of freedom) hand tracking for gesture controls; and it's all standalone, as there's no tether or wired puck handling the heavy lifting. With all that crammed into the frames, plus the battery to run it, you'd expect them to be heavy. At around 135 grams, they aren’t light, but Specs are surprisingly comfortable. The weight is distributed evenly, mainly across the frames, so for the brief time I used them, they remained ergonomically acceptable. Specs feel more like a pair of sunglasses than a bulky VR helmet. As for battery life, Snap promises four hours of mixed-use on a full charge. 
Display quality on Snap SpecsIn the interest of not alienating the people around you, Snap chose to make the lenses clear enough that your eyes can still be seen through them, but if you want to close out the world, there’s electrochromic dimming for quick transitions between clear and dark lenses. It both useful and a cool trick. Check it out:
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
The in-glasses display is surprisingly bright. Specs' visuals are powered by a proprietary liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) display system, and even when used in a light-filled conference room, I could still clearly see the UI and its various apps. I tested out YouTube under these borderline abusive conditions, and it streamed high-def video in 16 million colors suitably.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The display offers a 51-degree field of view. It feels like having a large floating window hovering in front of you. From there, you can use simple gestures to launch apps, watch movies, play games, and do most other tasks you can’t do from your phone. But it was the context-aware, real-world spatial computing tasks that I wanted to try—the things you can't do from a phone or PC. What can you actually do with a pair of Snap Specs? Snap plans to launch Specs with a full suite of both first-party and third-party apps that will do everything from improving your drawing skills to teaching you music. I tried out a golfing demo, and it made the possibilities of augmented reality glasses immediately clear. Instead of putting blindly toward a distant hole, Specs show you exactly which direction to swing the putter and adds a virtual flag to mark where the hole is. It’s anecdotal evidence, but my personal putting game improved immensely. Is it cheating? Probably, but it works. Are Specs going to be useful in the real world?A half-hour or so of testing a prototype isn’t enough time to really say whether these will be useful in a person’s real life, but I can say for sure that they’re very cool, and I’m looking forward to going more in-depth with them in the coming months as their release date approaches. Snap Specs are planned for release this fall and will retail for $2,195.

title: If Your iPhone 18 Pro Is Randomly Rebooting, There's a Fix Coming
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max users are reporting random reboot issues with their devices.
                                            These new iPhones reportedly freeze up after a failed Face ID attempt, and reboot shortly after.
                                            Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and Ultra 4, also have reboot issues of their own.
                                            Apple released a patch for Apple Watches on Wednesday, and an update is in the works for iPhone 18 Pro users.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple released a bunch of new devices last week. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 support new health-tracking features and Siri AI, while the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max introduce the A20 chip and variable aperture for the first time on Apple's smartphones. But while all these new products are objective upgrades over their predecessors, they all have one issue in common: They keep randomly rebooting. 
What is Apple's rebooting problem?As reported by 9to5Mac, some iPhone 18 Pro users are noticing that their smartphones are freezing up after a failed Face ID scan. When this happens, you won't be able to interact with your iPhone, even if the "Try Face ID Again" button appears on-screen. After a few moments, the iPhone will reboot. It's not a catastrophic issue, but it is annoying, and it's affecting a number of users, as this Reddit thread shows. It's a similar story with the latest Apple Watches. While the Series 12 and Ultra 4 obviously don't use Face ID, users are still experiencing random reboots—emphasis on "random." Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro users, affected Apple Watch users aren't doing anything in particular when their watches reboot. They could be in the middle of a workout, chatting with Siri AI, or using the Maps app, when all of a sudden, the Apple logo appears. Some analyses showed that the Neural Engine was at fault, but Apple never confirmed the exact issue.  
Apple has fixes in the works for iPhone 18 Pro usersThat said, Apple did find solutions to the reboot issues on all of these devices, though only the Apple Watch has a current fix. Apple released watchOS 27.0.1 exclusively for Series 12 and Ultra 4 users on Wednesday, which it says should fix random reboots going forward. And while iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max users don't have a fix yet, Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that an update is in the works.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As such, don't feel the need to take your new iPhone 18 Pro to the Apple Store if your only issue is random rebooting. While some Apple Store employees have swapped out affected units, the upcoming software update should be enough to take care of the issue. While we don't have an exact ETA for the update, expect it to be called something like iOS 27.0.1, similar to watchOS 27.0.1. And if you want to ensure you update as soon as it's available, regularly check for it in Settings > General > Software Update.

    The following content is brought to you by Lifehacker partners. If you buy a product featured here, we may earn an affiliate commission or other compensation.
    
            Credit: CleanMyMac
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You’re cruising through a work meeting when your boss asks you to share your screen. Your stomach drops. You have something like 15 tabs open, PDFs scattered from bezel to bezel, and four identically titled Excel spreadsheets to toggle between. Basically, your Mac’s desktop looks like your bedroom did in the eighth grade.While a messy desktop and digital clutter can be a source of anxiety for many people, it’s actually evidence of your deep work. Between an analyst keeping 15 tabs open so a model doesn't break and a strategist searching through 12 near-identical files right before a Zoom call, the clutter comes with the work.Running a standard cleanup app to achieve “desktop zero,” or digital minimalism, isn’t always the right solution. It assumes the mess is the problem, and it asks you to interrupt your workflow to fix something that isn’t broken. The fear of accidentally purging a vital draft or dataset is a pain point for anyone with years of research and work stored on their hardware.
An app like CleanMyMac by MacPaw that respects your working files and clears the system junk works the other way around: it's built to go after what's safe to remove, not the files you're actively using. MacPaw, known for user-friendly Mac software like ClearVPN and Eney, built its flagship CleanMyMac app to be a safe, quick way to tidy up your machine.
Where the slowdown actually comes fromYour open tabs aren’t the only thing slowing down your Mac; often, it’s the invisible stuff under the hood. Preview a dataset and a cache file writes itself somewhere you’ll never look. Open the same Slack PDF twice and you own two copies of it. Trial an app in March, abandon it in April, and its support files stay behind. None of it shows up on your desktop, but it’s all sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac tackles hidden hardware weight, OS health, and security threats while keeping you in control of your user assets. The app identifies potential clutter, such as old versions and duplicate downloads, without forcing you into tedious manual folder searches. It then shows you the results so you can review what it found and choose what to remove. The four spreadsheets stay put, because you’re the only one who knows which version is current.One scan, five kinds of dead weight
    
            
            
                                        Credit: MacPaw
                    
    
When you open CleanMyMac, the main tool you’ll see is called Smart Care. Click on it, and the software will automatically scan your Mac and purge invisible OS debris.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Here’s a rundown of what the app  does:Deep cleans: Utilizing Smart Selection technology, it intelligently targets and removes hidden background junk (outdated caches, temporary system files, and broken downloads) while respecting your personal work files.Scans for threats: Automatically scans for background malware and security threats to keep your online life safe.Boosts performance: Clears system memory (RAM) and tracks CPU loads to keep your Mac peppy during intense workloads.Runs updates: Flags outdated apps so you can update them, and when you want to delete them, it clears out hidden leftover files apps leave behind.Declutters storage: Deletes duplicate files (like those identical PDFs you’ve downloaded multiple times from Slack), similar photos, and forgotten large installer downloads taking up storage space.Plus, CleanMyMac’s Cloud Cleanup tool will reveal large files hogging up your cloud storage. And the app’s real-time monitors help ensure you always have space available for new files, PDFs, and research materials.Your working mess isn't the problem
    
            
            
                                        Credit: MacPaw
                    
    
A cluttered desktop, outdated files, and endless email chains aren’t the sign of a scattered brain. They’re evidence of deep, analytical work. What you don't know, and shouldn't have to, is how many gigabytes of cache files and abandoned app leftovers are sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac by MacPaw clears the background weight, so the only thing competing for your attention is the problem you're actually working on. If you're curious, there's a seven-day free trial to test it out on your own Mac.

title: How to Claim Your Piece of Apple's $250 Million Siri Settlement
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple agreed to settle a lawsuit over delays with Siri AI for $250 million.
                                            If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 device between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025, you may be eligible for a share.
                                            If you're an eligible claimant, it's now time to submit your claim.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, Apple released Siri AI, the company's biggest overhaul to its smart assistant ever. If you have a compatible device running the latest updates, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, you now have access to Apple's AI-powered Siri, in addition to a number of new Apple Intelligence features. For some of us, this might seem like a welcome upgrade from a company that hasn't done as much with AI as its competitors. For others, it's a long overdue fulfillment of a promise. So overdue, in fact, that Apple may be offering a payout to make up for it.Delays in launching Siri AI triggered a lawsuitThis year's iOS updates aren't the first we've seen of Siri AI. Back in 2024, Apple advertised a new AI-powered Siri that could understand content on your screen and pull data from your various apps to inform its answers. In Apple's pre-recorded demos, for example, Siri could dive through your texts and emails to locate a family member's travel information if you asked the assistant what time that person's flight arrived. Apple said this new Siri would arrive with iOS 18 later that year, launching on compatible iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 devices. But while the company slowly rolled out Apple Intelligence features through the iOS 18 lifecycle, this new Siri was nowhere to be found.For many, this absence ranged from mildly humorous to frustrating. Some, however, found it deceptive. After all, Apple said users who bought a certain iPhone could expect it to run this supercharged Siri. You might have picked up an iPhone 16, or perhaps the previous-generation iPhone 15 Pro, assuming you could take advantage of Apple's AI-powered assistant, but those changes didn't actually arrive until last week, more than two years after Apple first announced them. Depending on your upgrade cycle, you could be on your second or third smartphone since then. 
These grievances weren't confined to grousing on the internet. The Clarkson law firm filed a suit against Apple, alleging the company misled customers with these new Siri features. While the company has not admitted wrongdoing, it did agree to a $250 million settlement to put the case aside. And if you're eligible, it is now time to claim your share of the settlement. Not all iPhone owners are eligible for a slice of this settlement. Per the terms, only customers who bought an iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model (iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e) can claim a share. What's more, there's a specific timeline during which purchases are eligible: June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you bought your iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 between these dates, you can make a claim. To start, head to the settlement's official website, then choose "File A Claim." If you have a Claim ID and PIN, you can share them here. If you don't, you can still choose to file a claim online. You can share your iPhone's serial number, though if you don't have it, you can share your Apple Account email address and the number associated with your iPhone. Claims are open from today, Sept. 21, through Dec. 21. How much will you get in the Siri settlement?While $250 million sounds like a huge payout, the final amount likely won't be: The estimated payout is $25 per claimant, though that may change depending on the number of respondents. If there are fewer claims than expected, you may receive as much as $95. As MacRumors reports, the final approval hearing is on Feb. 24 of next year, so don't expect the money any time soon.

title: How to Get the Most Cloud Storage Possible for Free
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost. A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself. Google: 15GB of free cloud storageThe most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number. 
Apple iCloud: 5GB of free cloud storageiCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month. Microsoft OneDrive: 5GB of free cloud storageSimilar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment. Box: 10GB of free cloud storageBox offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents. Dropbox: 2GB of free cloud storageDropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps. Proton Drive: 5GB of free cloud storageProton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MEGA: 20GB of free cloud storageMEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media. Other cloud storage services: Free storage amounts varyThere are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services. Password managers often include free storageYour password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB. How to organize and maximize your free storage spaceIf you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box. Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

title: I Tried Google’s New Image Editor, and It Could Replace Canva and Photoshop
description:
Google Pics has arrived.
                                                    Credit: Google
                            
        
        Google launc
body:
Google Pics has arrived.
                                                    Credit: Google
                            
        
        Google launches (and retires) apps at a rapid rate, so it's not always easy to keep track of everything that's coming and going. One of the more recent launches we've had is Google Pics, which is now available to users subscribed to Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or Google AI Ultra ($99.99 or $199.99 a month).It sits alongside Google Docs, Slides, and Sheets in your Google Drive Workspace, and it's part Canva, part Photoshop: It does a bit of graphic design (like putting together an event poster), and a bit of image editing (like cutting unwanted objects out of your vacation photos), and if you're paying for one of those Google AI plans mentioned above, you might find Google Pics is the only image creation app you need.The web app incorporates the Nano Banana AI image generation model, and, as well as working as a standalone entity, will also pop up inside the other Google Workspace apps as and when you need it. Here's what you get and how it works.
How to use prompts with Google PicsGoogle Pics is driven primarily through text prompts, whether it's creating something new from scratch or making edits to something you've made elsewhere. From the opening screen, you can type in an image prompt just as you would with the Gemini app: Prompts for anything from photorealistic scenes to printed materials will work, and the more detail you add, the better.The Style box lets you give Google Pics a reference to work from in terms of the overall image look and feel, while clicking on the Upload, Drive, or Photos links lets you load in an existing image ready for editing. At the very top is an aspect ratio drop-down, so you can specify the dimensions of new images, though this can be edited later too.
    
            
            You can create new images or edit existing ones.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
When you make something new, you get four or five alternatives shown as thumbnails on the left, so you can click through them to find the one you want. There's also the option to generate four more pictures from your prompt, if you don't mind the extra usage. As it often is, Google is rather vague when it comes to limits: It says "higher access" will be available to users until February 2027, and that factors like image resolution affect how quickly you reach the limits.So, you could prompt Google Pics like this: "Create an A5 flyer for a 10th birthday party for Jess, happening at the village town hall at 3 p.m.-6 p.m. on Sunday, September 20. Include lots of party decorations, including balloons, streamers, and cake, and include some small print about food and drink being provided and there being plenty of on-site parking."From that prompt, Google Pics gave me a selection of suitable vibrant and fun-looking flyers I could choose from—all of them carrying that familiar AI "sheen" you've no doubt seen everywhere from restaurant menus to school event posters in recent times. It followed the brief directions and took seconds to do.
    
            
            Google Pics does graphic design and image editing.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
I also tried loading in my own photos and using Google Pics to manipulate them: You can very easily turn your photos into watercolors or comics, giving you what's effectively an unlimited box of Photoshop filters to play around with. The results aren't perfect every time, but they're usually more than good enough.This is a pretty bare-bones app though. You can undo recent edits, zoom in and out, and change the aspect ratio, but outside of the prompt box, that's just about it. You don't have any of the traditional resizing options or tools to do any drawing or touching up yourself, and there's no support for layers—so you're still going to need Photoshop and Canva around for more advanced tasks.How to edit images in Google PicsWhere Google Pics really impresses is with the editing tools, which become available after you've created something from scratch or loaded in an existing image. First of all, the app identifies parts of the image you can click on—so "church", "sky", and "mountains," for example. You can click on these specific elements to get a prompt box to make changes.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You can also just drag a box around something on screen to bring up a prompt box: Maybe drag a box around a party balloon and add the prompt "make this blue," or select a random stranger in your family vacation photo and say "remove this person". Any edit you can describe, you can make (or at least attempt).
    
            
            You're able to select specific image elements to edit.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
As always with this kind of trickery, Google Pics doesn't know what's actually behind the people and objects it's removing, but it can make a decent AI-inspired guess based on the rest of the image and background. The results I got were mostly fine, and usually you wouldn't know an edit had been made—though bigger changes to more detailed photos, like removing buses and cars, can be difficult for Google Pics to handle.You can save up all of these various edits and apply them together, which saves quite a bit of waiting and working forwards and backwards. In the case of my birthday party flyer, I was able to add lines of text, change various colors, add in new elements, and more—and if you select blocks of text, you can edit them directly without a new prompt.Besides being useful practically, it can also be a lot of fun playing around with different edits and seeing what's possible. I got quite addicted to playing around with different photos, making changes that ranged from the large scale ("turn this into a night scene") to the small scale ("add an extra cloud here").
    
            
            Image text can be edited directly.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One of the edits I made was to age a car in a scene by five years, something which I've got no idea how to do in a full image editor, and which would've probably taken me an hour or so even if I did. The end results might not be quite as precise or polished as they would be if done by a human hand, but these kinds of tools expand what's possible with quick and casual image editing.I won't be ditching Canva and Photoshop just yet, as they're still essential for different kinds of tasks, including projects where pixel-level precision is required and where various elements need to be combined together in layers—but I can also see Google Pics proving very useful, especially with its integration with the rest of Workspace.

title: Why You Probably Won't Have to Verify Your Age With Discord After All
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Discord is now rolling out its new age verification requirements. However, the company says the vast majority of users won't have to verify.
                                            Users will automatically be placed in "age groups" based on their account age and activity.
                                            If Discord gets it wrong, you can still verify your age through a number of methods, including face recognition and ID scans.
                                            While some of the methods are less risky than others, age verification is still fallible.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Discord age verification is officially here. As TechCrunch reports, the company will no longer take you at your word when it comes to how old you are, no matter where you happen to be using the app. Only verified adults can use Discord without restrictions; anyone under the age of 18 will be able to continue chatting on the platform, but with certain limitations. This change didn't come out of nowhere. Discord originally planned to roll out age verification en masse back in March, but the company quickly pivoted following backlash to its February announcement. That initial news lit the internet up with controversy, as it seemed that Discord was asking all users to upload a government ID to use the service as intended. While the company's plans were a bit more nuanced than that, the criticisms did force Discord  to adjust how it planned to approach age verification. Now, those rules are officially here, but the vast majority of users likely won't even notice anything has changed.    How Discord's age verification now worksThe first step, currently rolling out, is to place all users into an "age group." This entire process happens automatically, and requires zero intervention from users—including uploading IDs or other means of authentication. Discord will lconsider a series of identifiers to determine your age group, including how old your account is and what servers you're a part of. The company says it does not look at messages, calls, or content to make these determinations. Based on this initial analysis, you'll be placed into one of three categories: 
Adult Age Group: Discord has determined you are 18 or older and can use the platform without limits.Teen Age Group: Discord has determined you are between 13 and 17 years old. You can continue using Discord with "protections," while adult content and settings are no longer available. Unconfirmed: Discord cannot determine your age group, and you now have the same limitations as the Teen Age Group. New accounts also fall under this category until Discord's AI gathers enough data to make a determination. Discord is adamant that the vast majority of users will not have to verify their ages via anything other than this automatic method—the company says more than 90% of users will not be asked to confirm their age, which suggests Discord is quite confident in its models. If you fall into the latter two categories but you are in fact 18 or older, you can still verify your true age with Discord. Following the backlash to Discord's initial plans, you have a number of options for how to verify yourself, including:Credit Cards: Discord uses Stripe to check your credit card number to verify that an adult owns that card. Discord says it never sees your number. App Stores: Depending on your platform, you can let Apple or Google Play share your age range with Discord to verify your age. Your birthday isn't shared.Google Wallet: Discord can confirm your age using the pass set up in your Google Wallet, which is based on information from your passport. AgeKey: An independent age verification tool you can use with other services, not just Discord.Discord also still allows you to verify your age with either an ID scan or a "facial age estimation" (i.e., uploading a video selfie for an AI to determine your age). Discord says that it only receives your age from these data points: If you choose to scan your ID, the other data it contains is immediately deleted, while the selfie video never leaves your device. What limits do Teen Age Group accounts have on Discord?If you aren't 18, your account may face some changes due to this new policy. Discord says messages from non-friends now head to your message requests inbox by default, so you must review each manually. Only adult accounts can turn this setting off. Discord will also send you an alert before you accept a friend request from someone you have no mutuals with. While using Discord, you won't be able to see "sensitive" images; which images are sensitive is decided by the platform's sensitive content filters. You also won't be able to access age-restricted servers or channels, and you won't be able to run commands with age-restricted bots. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Age verification systems are fallible  While this policy is certainly an improvement over the one presented in Discord's February announcement, it obviously isn't perfect. Discord itself admits that its automated system may get it wrong, meaning that teens may be labeled as adults, or vice versa. Discord may force users 18 years or older to verify their identities when they never needed to before, which will especially sting for users who care deeply about their personal privacy.But it isn't just privacy-minded individuals who should be concerned. Age verification has been a bit of a disaster for several of the companies that have started rolling it out. Roblox got into hot water after its age verification proved shockingly easy to bypass, letting kids continue to use the platform without limits. Meanwhile, IDscan.net lost over 150 million driver's licenses in a breach this month. Discord doesn't use IDscan.net, and instead relies on Veratad for its ID scan services—but a previous third-party partner, 5CA, was breached last year, exposing ID images.It's great that Discord has presented some alternative methods of verification, but anyone who chooses to verify via documentation still must send their government ID to a third-party party. Discord says your ID data is deleted once verification is complete, but the whole endeavor requires a lot of trust. All it takes is one weak link in the chain to risk exposing sensitive user records, all in the name of accessing age-restricted features. Yet this appears to be the new norm: More and more states are passing laws requiring age verification for at least some adult content on the web, while countries around the world are beginning to pass social media bans or set limits for minors. It doesn't seem like the unrestricted internet of the past will be around for much longer. Hopefully we don't end up compromising privacy and security in the process of keeping younger users safe.

        The Philips Wifi Keypad Door Lock with Handle is down to $104.47 from its usual $142.49 price, marking its lowest price so far, according to price trackers. For that price, you’re getting a smart deadbolt, keypad, fingerprint reader, app controls, and a matching handle set in one package. Many smart locks at this price only replace the deadbolt, so the included handle makes this feel like a more complete front-door upgrade without buying extra hardware. It runs on eight AA batteries, and those are not included.
The day-to-day convenience is the real reason to consider it—since it connects directly to 2.4GHz wifi, there's no separate bridge or hub to buy, plug in, or troubleshoot later. Once connected, you can unlock the door with your fingerprint, enter a PIN on the keypad, use the Philips Home Access app, or stick with a physical key when needed. The app is especially useful if you need to check whether the door is locked, see recent access history, or let someone in while you're not home—it lets you create different types of codes for different people, including one-time codes for guests or recurring codes for cleaners, dog walkers, or family members. It also works with both Alexa and Google Assistant, so checking whether the front door is locked can be as simple as asking a smart speaker.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Philips says the lock is designed for doors between 1⅜ and 1¾ inches thick, and installation should be manageable with a screwdriver, though replacing both a deadbolt and handle still takes some patience. Once installed, you can set it to re-lock automatically within zero to 180 seconds after closing. In all, this is probably more smart lock than you need if you only want a basic keypad. But if you want app control, fingerprint entry, guest codes, and a cleaner-looking handle set in one box, this Philips deal makes sense at just over $100.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        The Blink Outdoor 4 Floodlight Camera is down to $39.99 on Amazon, a sizable discount from its $99.99 list price and, according to price trackers, its lowest price to date. At that price, you're getting a home security camera and a motion-activated floodlight in one unit, which makes it an easy way to cover a backyard, a driveway, a side yard, or whichever corner of your property never seems to get enough light. The real appeal, though, is that there's no wiring to deal with, because both the camera and the floodlight run on batteries. That flexibility also extends to placement—since the camera connects over wifi, as long as you have a decent signal, you can install it without having to plan around a nearby outlet, notes this PCMag review.
The setup pairs a motion-activated floodlight with a 1080p camera, powered by four D-cell batteries and two AA batteries, respectively. Naturally, you’ll need to keep an eye on battery life over time and replace the batteries periodically, but it’s otherwise fairly straightforward. When the camera detects movement, the floodlight kicks on with up to 700 lumens of brightness, which should be enough to illuminate a driveway, side yard, or other dark area around the house, while the camera records in 1080p. It also has infrared night vision, so you can continue monitoring the area after dark even when the floodlight isn't on.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The bigger consideration is the ongoing cost if you want more than basic camera access. Blink’s subscription plans start at $3.99 per month for one device and $11.99 per month for unlimited devices, with cloud storage, video history, and advanced alerts among the features tied to the paid plans. You do get a 30-day trial to see whether those extras are useful before committing, but anyone who wants to keep recorded clips in the cloud should factor the subscription into the overall cost. For those who prefer local storage, you’ll need to purchase a Sync Module XR and a MicroSD card with up to 256GB of storage separately, since the included Sync Module Core doesn’t support local backups.
